verses.text: I ask then, did God reject His people? Certainly not! I am an Israelite myself, a descendant of Abraham, from the tribe of Benjamin.
God did not reject His people, whom He foreknew. Do you not know what the Scripture says about Elijah, how he appealed to God against Israel:
"Lord, they have killed Your prophets and torn down Your altars. I am the only one left, and they are seeking my life as well"?
And what was the divine reply to him? "I have reserved for Myself seven thousand men who have not bowed the knee to Baal."
In the same way, at the present time there is a remnant chosen by grace.
And if it is by grace, then it is no longer by works. Otherwise, grace would no longer be grace.
What then? What Israel was seeking, it failed to obtain, but the elect did. The others were hardened,
as it is written: "God gave them a spirit of stupor, eyes that could not see, and ears that could not hear, to this very day."
And David says: "May their table become a snare and a trap, a stumbling block and a retribution to them.
May their eyes be darkened so they cannot see, and their backs be bent forever."
I ask then, did they stumble so as to fall beyond recovery? Certainly not! However, because of their trespass, salvation has come to the Gentiles to make Israel jealous.
But if their trespass means riches for the world, and their failure means riches for the Gentiles, how much greater riches will their fullness bring!
I am speaking to you Gentiles. Inasmuch as I am the apostle to the Gentiles, I magnify my ministry
in the hope that I may provoke my own people to jealousy and save some of them.
For if their rejection is the reconciliation of the world, what will their acceptance be but life from the dead?
If the first part of the dough is holy, so is the whole batch; if the root is holy, so are the branches.
Now if some branches have been broken off, and you, a wild olive shoot, have been grafted in among the others to share in the nourishment of the olive root,
do not boast over those branches. If you do, remember this: You do not support the root, but the root supports you.
You will say then, "Branches were broken off so that I could be grafted in."
That is correct: They were broken off because of unbelief, but you stand by faith. Do not be arrogant, but be afraid.
For if God did not spare the natural branches, He will certainly not spare you either.
Take notice, therefore, of the kindness and severity of God: severity to those who fell, but kindness to you, if you continue in His kindness. Otherwise you also will be cut off.
And if they do not persist in unbelief, they will be grafted in, for God is able to graft them in again.

For if you were cut from a wild olive tree, and contrary to nature were grafted into one that is cultivated, how much more readily will these, the natural branches, be grafted into their own olive tree!
I do not want you to be ignorant of this mystery, brothers, so that you will not be conceited: A hardening in part has come to Israel, until the full number of the Gentiles has come in.
And so all Israel will be saved, as it is written: "The Deliverer will come from Zion; He will remove godlessness from Jacob.
And this is My covenant with them when I take away their sins."
Regarding the gospel, they are enemies on your account; but regarding election, they are loved on account of the patriarchs.
For God's gifts and His call are irrevocable.
Just as you who formerly disobeyed God have now received mercy through their disobedience,
so they too have now disobeyed, in order that they too may now receive mercy through the mercy shown to you.
For God has consigned everyone to disobedience so that He may have mercy on everyone.
O, the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are His judgments, and untraceable His ways!
"Who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been His counselor?"
"Who has first given to God, that God should repay him?"
For from Him and through Him and to Him are all things. To Him be the glory forever! Amen.

context.author: Paul the apostle, writing through a secretary named Tertius (1:1; 16:22)
context.genre: Letter (epistle), written as a carefully argued case for the gospel
context.audience: The Christians in Rome, a mixed community of Jews and Gentiles
context.setting: Paul asks, “Did God reject his people?” and answers no. There is a remnant, as in Elijah’s day, and Israel’s stumbling has opened the door for Gentiles. He warns Gentile believers not to boast, using the picture of a wild olive branch grafted into a cultivated tree, and he ends with a hymn of praise.
context.custom: Grafting wild branches into a cultivated olive tree was backwards, since farmers usually grafted good branches into wild stock. Paul says it is “contrary to nature” (v.24) on purpose, to show that God’s kindness is unexpected.
context.timelineImmediate: Chapter 12 starts the practical section with “Therefore,” turning from the long argument to daily living.
context.timelineBible: Paul cites Elijah at Mount Horeb (1 Kings 19:10, 18), Isaiah 29:10, Psalm 69, and Isaiah 59:20-21 for “the deliverer will come from Zion.” The closing hymn draws from Isaiah 40:13 and Job 41:11.
context.sparkNotes: God has not rejected Israel. A remnant believes now, and Israel’s failure brought blessing to the Gentiles. Gentile believers are like wild branches grafted into the olive tree and must not boast. A partial hardening has come on Israel until the full number of Gentiles comes in, and “all Israel will be saved.”

translation.meaning: Joined into a tree. The picture is of Gentile believers sharing the same life as the original branches.
A truth hidden for ages and now revealed. Here: Israel’s hardening is partial and temporary.

otBackground.note: God kept seven thousand who had not bowed to Baal.
The deliverer will come from Zion and turn Jacob from ungodliness.
“Who has known the mind of the Lord?”

overview.summary: God has not rejected Israel. Gentile believers are grafted into the root, and Paul expects Israel’s restoration. The chapter ends with praise for the depth of God’s wisdom.
overview.settingLine: Paul writes from Corinth to the Christians in Rome.

history.t: In a dark time, God kept seven thousand who had not bowed to Baal, the pattern for the remnant.
The Roman church had tension between Jews and Gentiles after Claudius’s edict.

customs.t: Olive trees took years to bear fruit and could live for centuries. They were a symbol of Israel (Jeremiah 11:16).
A first batch of dough offered to God made the whole lump holy (v.16).

archaeology.t: Olive trees in Gethsemane and elsewhere in Israel are very old, a picture of a living root.
Stone presses are found at many excavated sites in Israel and Greece.

overview.discussion: Paul warns Gentile believers against pride toward Israel. Where do I need the same reminder that I live on someone else’s root?
overview.book: The letter to the Romans · 16 chapters. Paul’s fullest explanation of the gospel, written to a church he had not yet visited.
overview.author: Paul

historicalImage.caption: Olive Trees, painted by Vincent van Gogh at Saint-Rémy in November 1889. Paul pictures Israel and the Gentiles as an olive tree (Romans 11:17-24).

currentImage.caption: One of the old olive trees in the Garden of Gethsemane, Jerusalem. Olives live for centuries and can be grafted, the picture behind Romans 11:17-24.
